1051.title: Food tells the journey
1051.hook: bagels, kubbeh, injera, shakshuka: the food follows the wanderings
1051.carry: a map of everywhere we've been
1051.howItsDone: Jewish families keep dishes from the places their families have lived, cook slow Shabbat stews such as cholent, dafina and hamin that need no fire on Saturday, and tell the story of the Exodus over the foods of the Passover seder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jewish humor, the two jesters in the market, and the line laugh. Did your gentle joke find the person who needed it? A new week starts in the kitchen. Day one thousand fifty-one.

Bagels. Kubbeh. Injera. Shakshuka. Say them out loud and you've crossed half a map. A ring of dough boiled and then baked. Dumplings of semolina or rice with meat folded inside, simmered in a sour soup. A soft, spongy flatbread for tearing and scooping. Eggs cooked in a pan of tomatoes and peppers. Each one sits on Jewish tables, and each one came from somewhere else, with someone. A family's food is a map of everywhere they've lived, and Jewish food tells that story plainly. Today's line: food tells the journey.
screen: `BAGELS, KUBBEH, INJERA, SHAKSHUKA.` → `HALF A MAP.` → `A FAMILY'S FOOD IS A MAP.`

segments.voice: The Torah already ties food to a journey. In Deuteronomy, a farmer brings the first fruits of the harvest in a basket and sets them down before the altar. He doesn't just hand them over. He has to tell a story, and it begins: "A wandering Aramean was my father." It goes on: down into Egypt, slavery, rescue, and finally this land and this fruit. The basket is the end of the journey; the words are the road that led there. The Haggadah later reads the same Hebrew another way, as an Aramean who tried to destroy our father, meaning Laban chasing Jacob. Two readings, one verse, and both of them a story told over food. The seder plate works the same way. Matzah, the bread of affliction. Bitter herbs. A meal you eat in order to remember a road. Then the laws of Shabbat shaped the stove itself. The Torah says: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." So Jewish cooks in lands far apart found a way to have a hot meal on Saturday without lighting a fire: a pot started before sundown on Friday, left to cook slowly through the night. Ashkenazi families call theirs cholent. Moroccan families make dafina. Sephardi families make hamin. Same law, different pots, depending on where the road went. And the dishes in today's hook trace those roads. Bagels from the Jewish bakeries of Eastern Europe. Kubbeh in the kitchens of Iraqi and Kurdish Jews. Injera on the tables of Beta Israel in Ethiopia. Shakshuka from North Africa. When families moved, they carried recipes the way the farmer carried his story. Today's line: food tells the journey.
screen: `A WANDERING ARAMEAN WAS MY FATHER.` · `A MEAL EATEN TO REMEMBER A ROAD.` · `NO FIRE ON SHABBAT, SO A SLOW POT.` · `RECIPES CARRIED LIKE A STORY.` · then, large: `FOOD TELLS THE JOURNEY.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: cook one dish with a story. You won't cook it right now. For now, sit and breathe, and go looking for the dish. Something a parent, a grandparent or a friend made, or something from a culture you love. Smell it in your memory. Hear the kitchen it came from. Then ask its story, the way the farmer had to tell his: where did this come from? Who carried it here? What changed along the way? Choose the day you'll cook it, and who you'll tell its story to while it's on the table. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for whoever carried it. The bell holds the time.
Cholent. The slow-cooked Shabbat stew Ashkenazi Jews started before sundown Friday, one of many names, dafina, hamin, for the same law of no fire on the Sabbath. Today's word.
Your line: a map of everywhere we've been. Today, at one meal, ask where one thing on the plate came from, and who brought it. Day one thousand fifty-one.

1052.title: Jewish music
1052.hook: klezmer, Sephardi songs, cantorial chant and new music
1052.howItsDone: Jews sing at the Shabbat table, hear the Torah chanted and the prayers led by a cantor in synagogue, dance to klezmer and other music at weddings, and keep Ladino, Mizrahi, Hasidic and new Jewish songs alive at home and in concert.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the farmer's basket and the slow Shabbat pot, and your line, a map of everywhere we've been. Did you ask where something on your plate came from? Today, what people sang while they traveled. Day one thousand fifty-two.

Late on a Friday night, the plates are cleared and the candles are low. Nobody says anything. Then someone at the end of the table starts humming. No words, just a line of sound: yai dai dai, rising and falling. Somebody joins on the second time through. Then a few more. A child taps the beat on the table. By the fourth time through, the whole table is singing a tune that has no words at all, and somehow everyone knows what it means. Today is about Jewish music, from that wordless tune to the wedding band and the synagogue.
screen: `THE PLATES ARE CLEARED.` → `YAI DAI DAI.` → `A TUNE WITH NO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Music is there from the start of the story. At the sea, after the crossing, Miriam takes a timbrel in her hand and the women follow her, dancing and singing. When King Saul is tormented, young David is brought to play the harp, and the spirit troubling Saul leaves him. And the Psalms keep asking for more: "O sing unto the LORD a new song." A new one. The psalm isn't content with the old tunes. In the synagogue, even reading is music. The Torah is chanted aloud, following small marks written above and below the words, and the cantor, the hazzan, leads the prayers in chant. Some cantors became famous for it, carrying a whole congregation on one held note. Then the music traveled with the people. In Eastern Europe, Yiddish-speaking musicians called klezmorim played at weddings, with clarinet and fiddle that seem to laugh and weep in the same phrase. Sephardi families, carried far from Spain, kept singing in Ladino, the Judeo-Spanish language: lullabies, love songs, wedding songs, often passed mother to daughter. Mizrahi singers carried the scales of Baghdad, Cairo and Sanaa. Hasidic communities treasure the niggun, the wordless tune from the Friday night table. Some Hasidic teachers said a melody can climb where words can't follow. And the music keeps arriving: choirs, rock bands, new settings of old prayers, the new song the psalm keeps asking for. Different instruments, different languages, different scales. Today's line holds all of it: the music.

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: listen to one Jewish song. In this sit, start by listening to what's already around you. The hum of a fridge. Traffic. Your own breath. Let the sounds rise and fall like a tune. Then, if you like, hum something low, no words, just a line of sound, the way the Friday night table does. Notice where it sits in your chest. Afterward, choose one Jewish song to hear today: a klezmer tune, a Ladino lullaby, a cantor's chant, a Mizrahi singer, a new song. If you pray, you can let the music carry your prayer without words. The bell holds the time.
Jewish music. Miriam's timbrel, the chanted Torah, klezmer, Ladino songs, Mizrahi scales, the wordless niggun, and the new song still being written. Today's word.
Your line: the music. Today, play that one Jewish song all the way through, and send it to one person who might love it. Day one thousand fifty-two.

1053.title: Repairing the world
1053.hook: Jews across communities speak of repairing the world through justice and service
1053.howItsDone: Jewish communities speak of tikkun olam in volunteering, giving and social justice work, in the Aleinu prayer said at the end of services, and in the teaching that the commandments themselves help set the world right; communities weigh these differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jewish music, from Miriam's timbrel to the wordless niggun, and the line the music. Did you send one song to someone? Today, two Hebrew words with a long road behind them. Day one thousand fifty-three.

Two Hebrew words turn up on banners at food drives. On youth group T-shirts. In sermons about hunger, refugees, the climate. Tikkun olam. Repairing the world. Some people hear them as a modern slogan, something a committee came up with. But these words are old, and the road they took to reach a T-shirt runs through a law court, a prayer said at the end of services, and a mystical teaching about scattered light. Today's word is tikkun olam, and it has more layers than the banner shows.
screen: `BANNERS, T-SHIRTS, SERMONS.` → `TIKKUN OLAM.` → `OLDER THAN THE BANNER.`

segments.voice: Tikkun means repairing, or setting right. Olam means world. The phrase appears in the Mishnah, in a chapter about divorce law, and it's surprisingly practical. A husband who had sent his wife a divorce document could once cancel it before a court in another town, without her knowing. She might remarry, believing she was free, when she wasn't. Rabban Gamliel the Elder put a stop to that, and the Mishnah gives the reason: for the repair of the world. The same reason is given for other rulings that close loopholes and protect people who could be harmed. So the first layer is legal. Repairing the world means fixing the rules so the vulnerable aren't left exposed. The second layer is prayer. The Aleinu, said at the end of services, looks toward a day when the world will be set right under the sovereignty of God. Repair, there, is a hope as wide as the whole earth. The third layer comes from the mystics of Safed. In a teaching that tradition links to Rabbi Isaac Luria, divine light was scattered into the world in sparks, and each good deed and each commandment lifts a spark back up. Every small act becomes part of mending something cosmic. And then the modern layer: justice and service. The Torah's line sits underneath it: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." Jewish communities lean on these layers differently. Some put social justice at the center. Others say the commandments themselves, prayer, Shabbat, study, are how the world is repaired. Some hold both. And the Mishnah adds a line from Rabbi Tarfon, here in paraphrase: it isn't on you to finish the work, and you aren't free to walk away from it. Today's line: repair the world.
screen: `A LOOPHOLE CLOSED IN A COURT.` · `A PRAYER FOR A WORLD SET RIGHT.` · `SCATTERED SPARKS LIFTED UP.` · `JUSTICE, JUSTICE SHALT THOU FOLLOW.` · then, large: `REPAIR THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: volunteer for one hour. The hour comes later. This sit is for choosing it. Breathe slowly, and let one thing in your neighborhood that's broken come to mind. A lonely neighbor. A food bank that's short-handed. A park full of litter. A child who needs help reading. Don't try to fix the whole world. Rabbi Tarfon already let you off that. Just choose one hour and one place. Picture yourself walking in the door. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for strength for that hour. If you don't, simply hold the picture and decide. The bell holds the time.
Tikkun olam. Repairing the world: a court's reason for protecting the vulnerable, a prayer's hope, scattered sparks, and justice and service today. Today's word.
Your line: repair the world. Today, put that one hour on your calendar, with a time and a place, so it isn't just a hope. Day one thousand fifty-three.

1054.title: The synagogue today
1054.hook: synagogues of every size and style, from shtiebels to cathedrals
1054.howItsDone: Jews gather in synagogues of every size for prayer, Torah reading, study, celebrations and mourning; some prayers need a minyan of ten, services can be led by any knowledgeable member, and some congregations also stream services online.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tikkun olam, from a court in the Mishnah to the food drive, and the line repair the world. Did your one hour get a time and a place? Today, the room where much of Jewish life gathers. Day one thousand fifty-four.

Up a narrow staircase, past a rack of coats, there's a room about the size of a living room. A bookcase bursting with worn volumes. A small cabinet against one wall. Folding chairs that don't match. Men and women are drifting in on a weekday morning, nodding hello. Across town stands a building with a great dome, tall windows and seats for a crowd. And somewhere else, a laptop is open on a kitchen table, with a grid of faces waiting to begin. All three are synagogues. Today: the synagogue, as it is now.
screen: `A ROOM UP A NARROW STAIRCASE.` → `A GREAT DOME ACROSS TOWN.` → `A GRID OF FACES ON A SCREEN.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew, a synagogue is a beit knesset, a house of gathering. That's the heart of it. Not first a building, but people coming together. The Torah sets the pattern when God tells Moses: "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them." Some readers linger on the last words. Not dwell in it. Among them. Later, the prophet Ezekiel tells the exiles that God will be to the scattered people "as a little sanctuary". The Talmud reads that as the synagogues and houses of study wherever Jews live. A little sanctuary, carried into every land. So what makes one? Not size. The Mishnah says certain parts of the service, like reading the Torah aloud to the congregation, need ten people, a minyan. Nothing there requires a rabbi. A knowledgeable member can lead the prayers. Inside, there's usually an ark holding the Torah scrolls, a lamp kept burning that recalls the lamp in the ancient sanctuary, and a reading table. Synagogues are traditionally built to face Jerusalem. Then the styles spread out. A Hasidic shtiebel, a small room used as a synagogue, full of books, study and prayer. A grand domed building with a choir. A Sephardi synagogue with the reading table in the middle and seats around it. Orthodox synagogues seat men and women separately; Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist synagogues usually seat families together. Some communities meet in a rented hall, a home or online. Each one is a house of gathering in its own way. Today's line: the gathering place.
screen: `BEIT KNESSET: A HOUSE OF GATHERING.` · `DWELL AMONG THEM.` · `A LITTLE SANCTUARY IN EVERY LAND.` · `TEN PEOPLE, AND NO RABBI REQUIRED.` · then, large: `THE GATHERING PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: visit a synagogue, even online. For this sit, start with a gathering you know. Breathe, and bring to mind a room where people you care about come together: a kitchen, a team, a place of worship of any kind. Notice what makes it feel like a gathering place. The faces? The sounds? The way people greet each other at the door? Then think of a synagogue near you, or one that streams its services. Choose a time this week to step in or log on, as a guest who simply wants to see. Calling ahead is a kind thing to do. If you pray, you can pray in your own words for the people who gather there. The bell holds the time.
Beit knesset. Hebrew for a house of gathering: the everyday word for a synagogue, whether a small shtiebel, a domed hall, or a screen of faces. Today's word.
Your line: the gathering place. Today, find the website of one synagogue near you, and look at what happens there this week. Day one thousand fifty-four.

1055.title: Yahrzeit
1055.hook: on the anniversary of a death, a candle burns through the day
1055.howItsDone: On the yahrzeit, kept on the Hebrew date of death, Jews light a memorial candle at sundown that burns through the next day, and mourners often say the Kaddish in synagogue with a minyan, visit the grave, give charity or study in the person's memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, beit knesset, a house of gathering of every size, and the line the gathering place. Did you look up one nearby? Today the path turns from Jewish life now to remembering. Day one thousand fifty-five.

On a kitchen counter, away from the curtains, sits a short white candle in a plain glass. It was lit at sundown. Nobody is eating by its light, and nobody will blow it out. It will burn through the night and the whole next day, until it goes out on its own. The person who lit it walks past it while making coffee, while answering the phone, while the kids argue about homework. Every time they pass, they see it, and they remember a face. A parent, maybe. Today's word is the name for this day.
screen: `A WHITE CANDLE IN A PLAIN GLASS.` → `NOBODY BLOWS IT OUT.` → `EVERY TIME THEY PASS, A FACE.`

segments.voice: Yahrzeit is a Yiddish word, the word Ashkenazi Jews use for the anniversary of a death. Sephardi families have their own names for the same day. It's kept for parents above all, and for others a person mourns. Why a candle? The tradition points to a verse in Proverbs: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." A small flame, steady and quiet, stands in for a life. Here's a detail worth knowing. The yahrzeit is traditionally kept on the date of death in the Hebrew calendar, not the everyday one. The Hebrew calendar's months follow the moon, so the day slides around on the wall calendar from year to year. Families keep a note of it, or a synagogue sends a reminder. That's why today's line is so plain: remember the date. Remembering takes a little planning. On the day, mourners often go to synagogue to say the mourner's Kaddish with a minyan, the ten from yesterday. The Kaddish is a prayer in Aramaic, and it doesn't mention death at all. It praises God's name. Mourners stand in front of the community and say, in effect, we are still here, and we still praise. Some people visit the grave. Some give to charity in the person's name. Some study a passage of the Mishnah; tradition notes that the Hebrew letters of Mishnah can be rearranged to spell neshamah, soul. And some just sit with the candle, and tell a story about the person to anyone who'll listen. Different families, different ways. One thing is shared: the date comes back each year, and someone keeps it.
screen: `A YIDDISH WORD FOR A YEARLY DAY.` · `THE SPIRIT OF MAN IS THE LAMP.` · `THE HEBREW DATE, NOT THE WALL CALENDAR.` · `KADDISH, CHARITY, STUDY, A STORY.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE DATE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: light a candle for someone. If you have a candle and a safe place for it, you can light it now. If not, picture the flame. Breathe slowly. Bring to mind one person who has died, someone you loved, or someone whose life mattered to you from a distance. See their face. Hear their voice saying something ordinary. Let the flame stand for them, small and steady. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, or say the Kaddish later with a congregation. If you don't, simply say their name once, out loud. The bell holds the time.
Yahrzeit. The yearly anniversary of a death, kept on the Hebrew date with a candle that burns through the day, and often with the Kaddish. Today's word.
Your line: remember the date. Today, write down the date of one loss that matters to you, somewhere you'll see it next year. Day one thousand fifty-five.

1056.title: Remember
1056.hook: memory is a commandment in Judaism
1056.carry: a memory that leads to doing
1056.howItsDone: Jews keep the command to remember through Shabbat, the Passover seder, the reading of the Amalek verses on Shabbat Zachor before Purim, Yizkor memorial prayers, yahrzeit candles and Holocaust remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the yahrzeit, a candle on the Hebrew date, and the line remember the date. Did you write one date down where you'll find it? Today, the word underneath that candle. Day one thousand fifty-six.

Can you order someone to remember? You can tell a person to stand up, or to sit down, or to be quiet. But memory seems to come and go on its own. A song on the radio brings back a summer. A smell brings back a grandmother's hallway. Nobody commands that. And yet the Torah does exactly this. Again and again, it doesn't say try to remember, or it would be nice to remember. It says, in the form of a command: remember. Today's word is that command, and it's one Hebrew word: zachor.
screen: `CAN YOU ORDER A MEMORY?` → `A SONG, A SMELL, A HALLWAY.` → `THE TORAH SAYS: REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Zachor is the command form of the Hebrew verb for remembering. It sits right inside the Ten Commandments in Exodus: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Notice what follows the remembering. To keep it. Memory in the Torah isn't a mood. It leads somewhere. The pattern starts with God. In the flood story, the text says: "And God remembered Noah." And the next thing that happens is a wind over the earth, and the waters begin to go down. In the Torah, when God remembers, something moves. That's the shape of zachor. Remembering is the first half of an act. Moses, near the end of his life, sings to the people: "Remember the days of old." Ask your father, he says, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will explain. Memory isn't stored in a book alone. It's passed hand to hand. There's a harder zachor too. Deuteronomy says: "Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way as ye came forth out of Egypt." Amalek attacked the weak and weary at the back of the line, and the passage closes with "thou shalt not forget." On the Sabbath before Purim, tradition reads those verses aloud in synagogue, and that Sabbath is called Shabbat Zachor. Remembering, there, includes remembering cruelty, so as not to look away from it. That word carries all the way to now. In the Yizkor memorial prayers, in Holocaust remembrance, in the candle from yesterday, the command keeps working. Shabbat, the road out of Egypt, the people who came before, what was done to the weak: in each, the Torah pairs remembering with doing. Today's line is one word: remember.
screen: `REMEMBER THE SABBATH, TO KEEP IT.` · `GOD REMEMBERED NOAH, AND A WIND.` · `REMEMBER THE DAYS OF OLD.` · `REMEMBER WHAT AMALEK DID.` · then, large: `REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: write down one memory. The writing comes right after the bell. For now, sit and breathe, and let one memory rise. Something you were told by an older person, or something you saw that you don't want lost. Hold it in detail: where you were, what the light was like, the words someone used. Ask Moses's question of it: who told me this, and who will I tell? If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the people who handed it to you. When the bell sounds, write it down, even in three plain lines. The bell holds the time.
Zachor. Remember: the Torah's command, for Shabbat, for the days of old, for what was done to the weak, a memory that leads to action. Today's word.
Your line: a memory that leads to doing. Today, read the memory you wrote to one person, or send it to them, so it lives in two places. Day one thousand fifty-six.

1057.title: Each link
1057.hook: each generation passes the tradition to the next
1057.howItsDone: Pirkei Avot, which opens with the chain from Moses onward, is studied in synagogues and at home, and families pass the tradition on at home: at the Shabbat table, at the Passover Seder, and in stories told to children and grandchildren.

segments.voice: Yesterday, zachor, and your line: a memory that leads to doing. Did you write down one memory before it slipped away? This is the week's last day: food, music, repair, the synagogue, a candle, a memory. Today, how all of it gets from one pair of hands to the next. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

Moses received the Torah from Sinai, and handed it on to Joshua. That is how Pirkei Avot begins, the part of the Mishnah whose name means the Chapters of the Fathers. It does not open with a law, or a blessing, or a wise saying. It opens with a relay. Joshua hands it to the elders. The elders hand it to the prophets. The prophets hand it to the men of the Great Assembly. Nobody in that sentence invents anything. Every person in it does exactly two things: receives, and passes on. Today's word is the place each of them stands.
screen: `MOSES RECEIVED IT, AND HANDED IT ON.` → `NOT A LAW: A RELAY.` → `RECEIVE, AND PASS ON.`

segments.voice: Each link. Tradition calls this line of hands shalshelet ha-kabbalah, the chain of tradition. Look at its two verbs. In Hebrew, Moses kibel, received, and masar, handed over. Received is a humble word. The Torah came to Moses; it didn't start with him. Handed over is a trusting word. It means letting go of something precious and putting it into someone else's hands. Then the Great Assembly speaks, and one of its three sayings is this: raise up many disciples. So the chain was never meant to be a single thread. Each link is told to reach toward many next links. The Torah itself puts the chain somewhere smaller than a school. In the Shema, Deuteronomy says, "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children", and then it names the places: sitting in your house, walking by the way, lying down, rising up. A kitchen counts. A car ride counts. Look back over this week and the same chain shows up in other forms. A recipe handed down. A melody. A candle lit on the right date. A memory written down so it won't vanish. None of it lasts by being admired. It lasts by being handed over. And a chain has one more thing to teach. Nobody holds the whole of it. Each link touches the one before it and reaches toward the ones after, and that small reach is the whole job. That's today's line: each link.
screen: `RECEIVED, AND HANDED OVER.` · `RAISE UP MANY DISCIPLES.` · `TEACH THEM UNTO THY CHILDREN.` · `A RECIPE, A MELODY, A CANDLE.` · then, large: `EACH LINK.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: tell one family story. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring up one story from your family: how two people met, how someone arrived in a new place, a meal, a mistake everyone still laughs about. It doesn't need to be important. Find the version you heard, the way it was told to you. Then tell it once in your head, slowly, with the details left in: the weather, the clothes, the exact words someone said. Notice which detail you would never want dropped. If you pray, you can give thanks for the person who handed it to you. If you don't, just hold their name for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Each link. One place in the chain of tradition: a person who receives and hands on, touching the one before and the one after. Today's word.
Your line: receives, and passes on. Today, tell one family story out loud to someone who hasn't heard it, and say who told it to you first. Day one thousand fifty-seven.
